iterations.theme: What every woman should know before childbirth: a conversation with Dr. Petra Podobnik about childbirth, empathy, boundaries and motherhood

sections.subtitle: Welcome to the Podobnik Specialist Hospital: from family heritage to a calling for life
sections.screenshot_description: Host Ana Radišić in the studio or hospital space introduces herself to podcast viewers, with Dr. Petra Podobnik sitting beside her in civilian clothing.
sections.content:
Host **Ana Radišić** opens a new episode of the podcast from the premises of the **Podobnik Specialist Hospital**, which she describes as a place where new lives are born every day and where children see the light of day in the hands of an expert team. She introduces her guest, **Dr. Petra Podobnik**, as a person who, as she says, „lives and breathes” this institution. Ana points out that Dr. Podobnik is filmed in civilian clothing, unlike the hospital setting where she is usually seen in her work coat, and concludes that she is a person who has matured both professionally and privately.

Dr. Podobnik thanks her for the invitation and emphasizes that she is glad the conversation will not concern medicine alone, but other topics as well. She first identifies herself as a mother, which she considers a transformative experience. Besides motherhood as the most important role at this time, she lists the health and well-being of her two children, a healthy and supportive partnership, and friendships and relationships with her loved ones.

**The origin of the medical path.** Speaking about how medicine entered her life, Dr. Podobnik explains that she grew up in a family in which both parents are doctors. Her mother is a neurologist, and her father has been a gynecologist for many years. Both first worked in state hospitals, where, as she notes, their dedication to the work was evident and the patient always came first. Only after eighteen years did they decide to run a private institution, which, as she stresses, is demanding and requires great sacrifice and physical presence.

The girl thus visited her parents at work from an early age, and she also knew the hospitals where they worked, Vinogradska and Merkur. This everyday familiarity with the medical environment, she says, becomes a normal part of life for children from medical families and often encourages the decision to study medicine. Apart from medicine, she also considered psychology and even veterinary medicine, but concluded that what mattered most to her was working with people.

**The number of babies born.** Ana Radišić cites the figure that around 6,500 babies came into the world in Dr. Podobnik's hands. Dr. Podobnik clarifies that she would not fully attribute that number to herself personally, but that over the past eighteen years more than seven thousand babies have been born in the maternity ward. She stresses that the number is not the most important thing to her, but rather being present with every woman.
keywords: presence with the woman in labor

sections.subtitle: No two births are the same: why an individual approach is the key to a woman's safety
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik explains to a patient, or shows a conversation with a pregnant woman during an examination, in a calm hospital setting.
sections.content:
Dr. Podobnik explains that in state institutions, because of the large number of patients, it is often impossible for a doctor to devote themselves physically to each pregnant woman as much as they would like. That is precisely why, she says, the Podobnik Specialist Hospital was designed as a place that exudes calm, with fewer patients, where each woman can be given attention.

Host Ana Radišić concludes that this is a completely individual approach, to which Dr. Podobnik replies affirmatively, but stresses that this requires time and cooperation. Her ideal scenario involves getting to know the patient over several meetings before the birth itself. She points out that patients who live outside Zagreb do not have to travel constantly, nor does she encourage them to, but it is good to gain insight into their way of thinking at least during the last few examinations.

At these meetings Dr. Podobnik tries to sense how the patient experiences pregnancy and childbirth, what her expectations are, and what her fears and wishes are. Only once she knows this can she adapt her approach to the patient's needs. Such an approach, in her words, creates the foundation of trust that is essential for a safe birth experience.

sections.subtitle: Empathy as the foundation of a good doctor and a psychotherapeutic approach in medicine
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić asks a question, while Dr. Petra Podobnik sits relaxed and looks at her interlocutor during a conversation about empathy.
sections.content:
Host Ana Radišić notes that Dr. Podobnik seems to be something of a psychologist and psychotherapist. Dr. Podobnik clarifies that she is not formally a psychotherapist, but that she has completed numerous educational programs and five years of training in body-oriented psychotherapy. She emphasizes that this served primarily her personal development and not to obtain a diploma, but that she applies the methods she learned to herself and to her patients.

Her interlocutor points out that these methods have helped her in her approach to life, in understanding herself and others, and also in working with patients, so she considers them immeasurably valuable. Ana Radišić concludes that a lot of empathy is expected of doctors in this work, which Dr. Podobnik confirms.

**Empathy as a prerequisite.** Dr. Podobnik believes that no one can be a good doctor in any branch of medicine without a certain dose of empathy. She acknowledges that people are born with different levels of empathy, but says that she herself has an exceptionally high level of empathy. That very fact, she explains, also brings a challenge, because she becomes too attached to certain situations, which can affect her mental state as well. That is why over the years she has learned to set boundaries in a healthy way: to be present and dedicated, but with the awareness that the patient also has her own story and that the doctor is not responsible for everything that happens in it.

sections.subtitle: Boundaries without guilt: how a doctor learns to say no and still remain dedicated
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik and Ana Radišić in conversation about setting boundaries, with emphasis on the guest's facial expression as she speaks about exhaustion.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić asks how difficult it was for Dr. Podobnik to learn to set boundaries, given that a doctor is responsible by nature and by profession, and works in a field of medicine that is especially sensitive because it concerns children and the arrival into the world. The host notes that even at the moment of filming a doctor may have „three or four channels” running in her head at the same time, since at any moment a new birth or a cesarean section may occur.

Dr. Podobnik replies that everything depends on which boundaries are meant. She says that she tries to do everything from the purest and best intentions for her patients and the people around her, but that sometimes she simply does not have the capacity, patience or energy. Boundaries, she says, often also mean not allowing someone who has different ideas, with which you do not agree, to needlessly consume your time and energy.

Regarding pregnancy and childbirth, she stresses that communication is key. The patient needs to say clearly what she expects, and the doctor needs to present her professional opinion on what would be best in the given situation. Mostly, she says, a shared solution is reached, although patients sometimes have a different plan that does not work out the way they imagined. In that case the patient must accept the situation, and it is essential that this be done with support and understanding.

**Boundaries at work.** When it comes to work, Dr. Podobnik believes it is necessary to set healthy boundaries so that extreme exhaustion does not occur. She admits that over the years she has learned to hand over some tasks to others, although she still likes to do many things herself, because she realizes that otherwise she runs out of time for activities that genuinely bring her joy. She concludes that life teaches us to set boundaries without a feeling of guilt, in a healthy way.

sections.subtitle: Fear of childbirth and traumatic experiences: how safety changes a woman's path
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik encourages a pregnant woman during an examination, with emphasis on the calm atmosphere in the examination room.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić notes that fears are one of the most common questions women ask before childbirth. Dr. Podobnik explains that every woman comes to childbirth with her life experiences, which shape her attitude toward pregnancy. Some women, she says, are not in a place where they can let go of control and relax, and that is precisely what childbirth demands most.

She stresses that medicine, despite its knowledge, ultrasound examinations and many methods, cannot predict everything or prevent certain situations. That is why, in her words, it is important to give patients a sense of safety and trust.

**Women with difficult experiences.** Dr. Podobnik особito emphasizes that in her practice she often encounters women who have gone through exceptionally difficult experiences: loss of a pregnancy, even multiple losses, loss in a later stage of pregnancy, or bad births that left deep fear. For such patients, she says, she especially tries to provide security. When a birth goes well and the woman feels peace and satisfaction, Dr. Podobnik experiences this as a privilege and the greatest fulfillment in her work.

sections.subtitle: When a doctor becomes a patient: her own birth and a lesson about unpredictability
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik sits opposite the host and speaks about her own birth experience, while Ana Radišić listens attentively.
sections.content:
Host Ana Radišić asks how Dr. Podobnik experienced her own birth, given that, being in medicine, she herself knows everything about the process. Dr. Podobnik admits that, despite her great knowledge, the most important realization was that nothing can be planned. At the time of her first birth she was not yet in the position she holds today, but she still knew that letting go of control had to be part of the experience.

Her son, who is fifteen years old today, was her first child and was born quickly and without major complications. Her daughter, now ten years old, was born later. Dr. Podobnik describes her experience as wonderful, although it was unpredictable.

**Advice for pregnant women.** It is precisely from that experience, she says, that she often advises her pregnant patients. Although women prepare throughout the entire pregnancy, often attend large courses and have an exact picture of how childbirth should look, life often shows the opposite. That is why Dr. Podobnik believes it is important to prepare not only for one specific scenario, but for whatever follows. She stresses that the medical team tries to take part in these preparations, but that the most important thing is for the birth, whether vaginal or by cesarean section, to go as well as possible for the mother and the baby, and for the feeling to remain that it was a beautiful, not a traumatic, experience.

sections.subtitle: The mother is the foundation of the child's safety: what truly matters in the first months
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić and Dr. Petra Podobnik talk about preparation for childbirth, and a course or education for future parents is visible in the frame.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić stresses that it is important for the mother to be well, because when she is well, the child is well too, and asks what would make a mother well and help her know how to act. Dr. Podobnik builds on this question and emphasizes that in the first year a child needs very little: to be dry, fed and, above all, in contact with the parents.

She says there is not much psychology in that period, and that parents often needlessly burden themselves with concepts that are not important in the first year. The baby should be held, carried and cuddled, and teaching it to be held and „spoiling” it is nothing bad. What matters is that the baby feels safety and calm, and if the mother is well and can devote herself to the child, the baby will be well too.

Dr. Podobnik also emphasizes that with the birth of a child a woman is also born into a new role, that of mother, and that the pressure from the environment on her is enormous. That is why it is important for the mother, as much as she can, to be rested, which is very difficult in the first months, and to have the support of her partner, family and loved ones.

sections.subtitle: What a baby needs in the first year: contact, safety and fewer rules
sections.screenshot_description: A young mother holds her baby in a calm hospital room, while Dr. Petra Podobnik explains the basic needs of a newborn.
sections.content:
Dr. Podobnik explains in detail what a baby needs in the first year of life. The basic needs are physical: to be dry, fed and cared for. The greatest need, however, is contact with the parents. She points out that people overly burden themselves with concepts that are not important in that period, whereas the baby should actually be held, carried and shown safety.

A baby who is especially in need must not be left to cry or raised according to strict rules, but should be given warmth and calm. Dr. Podobnik gives the example of her grandmother, who knew no psychology at all, but raised her children so that they were never left to cry, because that approach was natural to them. She says that later various strategies developed, such as mothers returning to work quickly or children being accustomed early to sleeping in their own room, which, in her opinion, is far from natural.

She concludes that the most important thing is for the baby to feel safety and love, and that in its upbringing one should not be guided by the pressures of society.

sections.subtitle: Pressure from the environment on mothers: expectations that exhaust and baby blues
sections.screenshot_description: A tired mother sits on the bed next to her baby, while Dr. Petra Podobnik explains how important it is for the mother to receive emotional support.
sections.content:
Dr. Podobnik warns that mothers today are under enormous pressure from their environment. Society imposes a number of expectations on them, and information is available at every step, from networks to various other sources. Mothers are, in her words, overloaded by these expectations, whereas what is essentially most important is for the mother to be as rested as possible and to have support.

Dr. Podobnik talks about how there used to be a „village” that raised the child. The baby was held by relatives, neighbors and family members, so the mother was not alone. Today such support is often absent, so mothers struggle to reconcile all the expectations and obligations.

In the first days and weeks, mothers often go through baby blues, a natural drop in hormones that makes them cry easily and feel emotional. Dr. Podobnik stresses that in this period it is important for mothers to be listened to, to feel support, and for their condition to be accepted as normal. This, she says, is what healthcare workers can provide, and mothers should continue to receive such support.
keywords: the village that raises the child

sections.subtitle: Why caring for the mother is just as important as caring for the baby
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić and Dr. Petra Podobnik sit in conversation, while a highlighted message about the importance of supporting the mother appears on screen.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić thanks Dr. Podobnik for the beautifully expressed thought and asks how she herself managed to reconcile all the expectations, given that she is at the same time a mother, a gynecologist and the daughter of a well-known doctor. The host recalls that Dr. Podobnik inherited the high standards of her father, who left a great mark in gynecology, and that she was the first in the region to open such an institution, which is today the only one of its kind in Croatia.

Dr. Podobnik admits that this was very difficult for her. The turning point was the birth of her son, because she then realized that she wanted to be the best possible version of herself for him. At that time she still did not have clear priorities or an awareness of her own purpose. She was, she says, torn in a hundred directions between work and motherhood, and it was difficult for her to firmly establish balance among the roles she had.

Regarding the chapter on expectations, it is also important that Dr. Podobnik stresses that caring for the mother is an integral part of caring for the child. If the mother is not well, it is hard for her to be good for the baby too.

sections.subtitle: From being torn to finding meaning: the path through motherhood, career and personal growth
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik sits and reflects during the conversation about her personal development and the moment she began working on herself.
sections.content:
Dr. Podobnik describes that, at the time when she was struggling with motherhood and various expectations, she came across by chance an education on natural parenting. She mentions that this is an approach based on natural principles, that is, on what is physiologically normal and what the baby truly needs. She also names the lecturer, **Tomislava Kuljiša**, who introduced her to these ideas, and the center that nurtured that approach.

She says she did not have time to read the numerous books, but simply believed what she heard, and it sounded true to her. She thus began to live that way in her private life as well. Gradually she realized that there is nothing wrong with a baby crying or demanding constant contact, and that the key is the parent's reaction and their inner state.

**Working on oneself.** Dr. Podobnik concludes that over the years of working on herself, together with the experience her job has brought her, she became calmer and found a better place for herself. That realization, she says, enabled her to perform her other roles with more peace and meaning.

sections.subtitle: Stories that remain: when the sense of community passes from colleagues to the audience
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić talks about the experiences of people from the team and acquaintances who experienced the birth of their children in this hospital, in the space where the podcast is recorded.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić relates that many people have passed through the corridors of this hospital and that it was right here that they experienced their most important life role. She mentions friends and acquaintances, but also people from the crew in the room, among whom were two men and two fathers who also had the experience of having children born in this institution. She assesses that such reactions are wonderful and show how deep an impression the institution leaves.

Dr. Podobnik confirms that such comments are valuable, but stresses that they are a consequence of the feelings the parents had. She says she felt particular happiness when she was able to witness such moments.

sections.subtitle: The greatest reward of the medical calling: when a woman is freed from fear
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik speaks with a smile about moments of joy after childbirth, while a calm room for new mothers can be seen in the background.
sections.content:
Asked what her personal greatest reward is, Dr. Podobnik replies that every birth is a moment of great joy, when parents experience the magical moment of their child's birth and their genuine happiness is visible. However, she says, she experiences the greatest satisfaction when she connects with a person who has gone through difficult experiences and when she knows that she was the one who changed her perception.

As an example she mentions women who have deep traumas and cannot physically or mentally decide on a new pregnancy, yet want a child. Our job, she says, is to give them safety, and once they have gone through that process, the experience can change their relationship to motherhood forever. It is precisely this, she concludes, that remains most significant in her work.

sections.subtitle: Childbirth at the Podobnik Hospital: calm, closeness and family in focus
sections.screenshot_description: A delivery room or postpartum room with a baby and family in a calm, warm setting.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić notes that, according to what she has read, childbirth in this hospital takes place in a more humane way. Dr. Podobnik confirms this, but stresses that it is an ideal that should be available everywhere. She points out that such an approach is unattainable in many systems, primarily because of the large number of patients.

She names a sense of calm as an important advantage. The woman in labor does not have to listen to many other women in different phases of labor, but can devote herself to her own experience. After the birth, in a room with the baby and family, intimacy is created and an opportunity for the parents to bond with the child. Dr. Podobnik concludes that such an experience should be the standard in any hospital, and that in some countries such conditions are already being achieved.

sections.subtitle: What love means to a doctor: from family to one's own being
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić asks a question about love, while Dr. Petra Podobnik answers in a thoughtful tone with a warm facial expression.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić asks Dr. Podobnik what love is to her, since she dedicates herself to her work with enormous love. The host adds that, in her opinion, it is the task of all people to spread love in the world.

Dr. Podobnik replies that love is the essence of everything. Love relates to children, partners, friends, parents and people in general. She notes that love should be cultivated toward every person, but also respect and understanding for their problems.

**Love for oneself.** The greatest art, in her words, is love for oneself, and not out of selfish motives, but as the foundation on which everything else is built. Dr. Podobnik believes this is a lifelong task. When a person has a solid base of love for themselves, they do not act out of fear, but out of trust in life and the conviction that everything happens for a reason. Then, she says, they surround themselves with people who also radiate, and they more often experience good things, and they pass through difficult ones more easily and learn a great deal from them.

sections.subtitle: Lessons the faculty did not teach: what medicine teaches about life
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik sits in conversation and speaks about her own work habits and her experience from specialization.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić asks what medicine taught Dr. Podobnik that the faculty did not. Dr. Podobnik admits that she has always been eager for knowledge and that she studied a great deal at the faculty, which gave her strong work habits. Today, she says, she would tell herself to relax a bit more, because grades are not that important in the end.

In the early phase of her career, during her specialization, they worked a great deal, which was a time that demanded sacrifice. She does not regret it, because it gave her the foundation and experience that are very important to her today.

**The value of contact with people.** She describes her work as wonderful because of the daily contact with people. She is glad of the open doors, where she meets new couples, recognizes their fears and answers their questions. Sometimes patients come to her with serious diagnoses or poor prognoses that they heard from other doctors. After an hour of conversation, people often leave her room calmer. Dr. Podobnik explains that a doctor cannot always influence the outcome, but can influence how the patient feels and how much the doctor is with them in those moments.

sections.subtitle: Recharging the batteries: nature, family and exercise as the path to balance
sections.screenshot_description: Dr. Petra Podobnik in nature or on a walk with her dog and children, while green spaces and family moments are visible in the frame.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić asks how Dr. Podobnik recharges her heart's batteries, apart from work and motherhood. Dr. Podobnik replies that over time she has realized these are small things, and one of the most important is staying in nature. She is happiest when she has a free weekend and can go to Gorski kotar, where her grandmother and grandfather live and where she has a house. There, she says, she spent the happiest part of her childhood, so that place is especially dear to her heart.

When she cannot travel far because of work, she finds rest in short walks, time in nature in Zagreb, spending time with her children and dog, and training. Currently she tries to exercise several times a week, which helps her relax and find strength to go on.

She particularly emphasizes that the best thing a person can do is spend time with the people they love.

sections.subtitle: The hall of one's own life: a closing thought on presence and gratitude
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić and Dr. Petra Podobnik conclude the conversation with a farewell, while an announcement of the next podcast episode appears on screen.
sections.content:
Ana Radišić thanks Dr. Podobnik for the wonderful conversation and points out that they have received many messages. Although, as she says, they are not gynecologists and are not alone in medicine, she believes a lot from what was said can be applied in our own lives.

Dr. Podobnik concludes that it is important to be present in the moment one is in, because then everything somehow falls into place. Ana Radišić complements this with the claim that in the moment of childbirth nothing exists outside the operating room, and that in everyday life too we have the opportunity to be present, even if we are not literally in an operating room, we are in the hall of our own life.

The episode ends with thanks to the guests and viewers and an announcement of the next podcast episode.
keywords: the hall of one's own life
